catalog_quote: Muak Sa-aak is a tonal language, with three tones which will be described in this chapter. The tones are closely linked with syllable structure. [...] In Muak Sa-aak, there are three distinctive tones, a low tone, a checked tone, and a falling tone. All main syllables have one of these. Presyllables do not display tonal contrast; although speakers labeled them all as Tone 1, the fact that they routinely identified them as the same tone shows that there is no contrast in tone. (p. 61) [...] The presyllable in Muak Sa-aak has no contrast in the tone or the vowel. It serves essentially to place an open transition between consonants which are not permitted as consonant clusters. Therefore although the language is sesquisyllabic, it is actually very close to being monosyllabic. The word structure may be summarized as (C.).C(C)V(C)T. The most common syllable types are CVCT, C.CVCT, and CVT. (…

new_statements.quote: The presyllable in Muak Sa-aak consists of an initial consonant plus a very short vowel with predictable quality. [...] Since neither tone nor vowel quality are distinctive in presyllables, they will be transcribed with only the contrastive initial consonant and a period (.) to mark the syllable break /C./. (p. 56) [...] In Examples (131) to (133), the first syllable is probably not a presyllable, as the vowel quality is clearly [aː], and it has a more stress and length than is normal for a presyllable. (p. 60) — cf. Hall 2013: 35: 'there are three distinctive tones: a low Tone 1, a checked Tone 2, and a falling Tone 3. All main syllables have one of these. Presyllables do not display tonal contrast'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-stress rule is stated anywhere in Hall's four descriptions. Muak Sa-aak is described as a three-tone, isolating, mono-/sesquisyllabic language: every main syllable (the final full syllable of a word) carries one of three lexical tones, while presyllables have a non-contrastive very short vowel and no tone. The single passing remark that a full /ʔaː¹/ syllable has 'more stress and length than is normal for a presyllable' implies that prominence falls on the main syllable and presyllables are weak, i.e. the usual iambic sesquisyllable, but this is never formulated as a stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: The /ʔaː¹/ initial of locative words 'there', 'where' (and 'drop') is a full syllable, not a presyllable (p. 60). Presyllables beginning with /s/ may reduce to a syllabic consonant in fast speech (§6.2.3). Tai Lue loans are extensive and reshape tone distribution (Hall 2014 MKS 43.1).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: citation forms from a ~1,700-item wordlist elicited from four speakers of Wan Fai village, Mong Yawng Township, eastern Shan State (2007-2008). Compounds are common and each member keeps its tone (Hall 2013: 28). Nothing on phrase-level prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Hall's data are from the Wan Fai (Wan Fan) village variety of Muak Sa-aak, Mong Yawng Township, eastern Shan State, Myanmar. Glottolog names tail1246 "Muak"/"Tai Loi" (tlq); "Tai Loi" is a Shan exonym applied to several Palaungic groups, and Hsiu 2015 (cited on the Glottolog page) equates tlq with Muak Sa-aak. Hall classifies it as Angkuic (Eastern Palaungic), alongside Hu and U (Svantesson 1988, 1991). Hall notes dialect variation between villages (e.g. diphthongs vs /ɛː, ɔː/) but describes one village only.

sources.note: No stress/accent section or rule. Ch. 4-5: words are mono-/sesquisyllabic, (C).C(C)V(C)T; three lexical tones (low T1, checked T2, falling T3) on every main syllable; presyllable vowel and tone are non-contrastive (pp. 54, 56); Muak Sa-aak is Thomas's Type (i) sesquisyllabic, 'closest to being a monosyllabic language' (p. 57). Only use of the word 'stress': p. 60, /ʔaː¹/ in 'there/where' words 'has a more stress and length than is normal for a presyllable' (implying presyllables are weak relative to main syllables).
